There's something quietly thrilling about the half-hour before sunrise. The sky isn't dark anymore, but it hasn't committed to being light. Everything exists in a soft, undecided gray — the trees are silhouettes without color, the air holds that particular coolness that feels like an invitation, and the whole world seems to be holding its breath. I think most people sleep through it, which is understandable. But I've always been drawn to liminal spaces — thresholds, in-between moments, the places where one thing hasn't yet become another.



Liminality is everywhere once you start looking. A bridge between cities. A hotel room on a business trip. The last week of December. The moment between hearing something funny and actually laughing, when your face is already rearranging itself before sound arrives. Even this — a blank page waiting to hold words that haven't been written yet — is a kind of threshold.



I think we're uncomfortable with in-between states because they demand something from us. Certainty is easy. A finished painting, a decided election, a closed door — these things ask nothing of you except acceptance. But a moment still in motion? That requires you to be *present*, to tolerate ambiguity, to sit with the discomfort of not yet knowing how the story resolves.

Maybe that's why I enjoy writing like this. No outline. No destination. Just the pleasure of sentences unfolding in real time, each one a small crossing from silence into meaning, and then back again when I eventually stop. There's a strange freedom in letting go of the need to arrive anywhere specific.
